title: The Fredo Job: the sound
intro: Round 1, sound only: the look and picture are locked and the crew's voice is picked (en-gb-concierge-10). Two Suno takes per sound (the first links on each card), then the real tracks that inspired it. Takes run 20-50 s; the cut uses about 18 s. Mark This / Maybe / No and leave a note.
story: A crew in BadCode balaclavas plans a slick heist for a 10p chocolate frog.
They walk out of the smoke, slip the lasers "like butter" and lift it.
At the counter the tag says 39p: the price ran off while they planned.
A savings jar that rises with the price.
Swagger, then hope: slick heist feel, a deflating sting on 39p, a lift on the jar. Music and effects only, under one Liverpool voice, about 18 s.

sounds.name: 1960s spy swagger
sounds.pitch: Twangy baritone guitar, walking bass, brass stabs, vibraphone: the cool-crew walk. The 39p lands on a big brass chord that slides down like a sad trombone; the jar gets the strings swelling back up.
sounds.why: The swagger is built in, and its self-aware glamour is made for ridicule: the grander it sounds, the smaller the frog.
sounds.risk: The obvious pick. Suno drifts towards one famous spy theme, which the parody rule forbids; it must stay generic. Its 'hope' is grand rather than warm.

sounds.name: Hard funk groove
sounds.pitch: A locked one-chord groove on the one: chicken-scratch guitar, slapped bass, horn stabs cut to every move (the tap, the step, the duck). The groove stops dead on 39p (needle off); it drops back in, brighter, on the jar.
sounds.why: The library names it for heists and comic swagger; a loop that never changes is the cleanest bed under a few spoken lines, and a dead stop is the best sting.
sounds.risk: Can feel like a period pastiche with no modern edge; little room for warmth, so the hope has to come from the groove returning, not from a melody.

sounds.name: British library cue
sounds.family: Novelty, found sound and the margins
sounds.pitch: A 1970s KPM-style jazz-funk cue (Hammond, wah guitar, fuzzy bass, brass fanfare) that sounds like a TV caper from British telly. The sting on 39p is a 'tension' cue; the jar gets a 'Happy Ending' button.
sounds.why: British where the heist genre is American, so it fits a corner shop and a Liverpool voice; it plays the joke as a cheap TV thriller.
sounds.risk: Can tip into nostalgia telly and feel dated rather than slick; Jack asked for heavy heist-film swagger and this is its small-screen cousin.

sounds.name: The corner-shop break (invented for this short)
sounds.family: Off the library: breakbeat heist score + found sound
sounds.pitch: A modern big-beat heist groove (a dusty drum break, organ, scratched record, low strings) where the shop is part of the band: the till drawer is the snare, the coin jar the shaker, the shop-door bell the hook. On 39p the record winds down; the jar fills with coins tuned up a major chord, and the beat comes back.
sounds.why: The slickest of the options, closest to the turn-of-the-century heist film Jack named, but made of the corner shop, so it's ours and never that film's score. The coins carry the way out in the sound itself.
sounds.risk: The most work: Suno makes the groove, the shop sounds are cut in by hand on the timeline. Too many effects can muddy the spoken lines.

sounds.name: Tiptoe cartoon caper (invented for this short)
sounds.pitch: Sneaking music: pizzicato strings, a muted sax and bassoon on tiptoe, every step hit on a plucked note, the laser duck a held breath. 39p gets a deflating tuba 'wah-wah'; the jar a warm clarinet lift.
sounds.why: The laughiest: it says 'these lot are clowns' and lets the 39p land as a gag. The swagger becomes sneaky swagger.
sounds.risk: Undercuts the 'played straight' brief: it tells the audience it's a joke before the twist does. The sad-trombone sting is a cliché.

sounds.name: Colliery brass band (against the grain)
sounds.family: British and Irish folk and roots
sounds.pitch: A northern brass band plays the job as a proud slow march, cornets and side drum, deadly serious. 39p: the band falters, one euphonium left. The jar: the whole band back in as a hymn, the way out sounding like a win for working people.
sounds.why: The strongest 'hope' of all of them, and the most British; it reframes the crew as ordinary working people, which is the point.
sounds.risk: The library says it undermines comedy and fast rhythm: little swagger, and the cuts can't land on fast hits. It may feel like a different film from the picture.

sounds.name: Clockwork pulse (against the grain)
sounds.pitch: Ticking marimba and piano in steady eighth notes, the plan as a machine, building in layers with every clip. 39p: one wrong note and it all stops. The jar: the pulse restarts and climbs, price and savings rising together as one harmonic climb.
sounds.why: The way out is a mechanism (money that keeps up), and this is the only sound that makes it one; the pulse leaves every spoken line clear.
sounds.risk: Clever rather than swaggering: it loses the cool-crew feel Jack asked for, and minimal music can feel like an advert for a bank.
